_meta.json_strictness_warning: S6 hygiene forward-pointer (T10 review, minor): this file is NOT strict JSON -- it contains three bare `Infinity` literals (google-benchmark's own output; see 'note' below for where and why) in a position strict RFC 8259 JSON forbids. Today's only reader is a human (per 'policy' above), so this is harmless, but any FUTURE machine consumer must use a lenient parser (Python's json module accepts Infinity/-Infinity/NaN by default) or must respell those three values (e.g. a very large finite sentinel, or a null with a sibling flag) before parsing with a strict parser (nlohmann::json rejects them by default) -- do not assume `Infinity` round-trips through every JSON library just because this file already has it.
_meta.seeded_by: S6 Task 10 (GPU sweep + per-pass Vulkan timestamps + baselines re-seed, spade/s6 plan): BM_StepPlainBodiesGpu/{10,100,1000} and BM_StepQuadWorldsGpu/{1,4,16,64} added to bench_sim.cpp, mirroring the CPU families' own builders exactly (build_plain_bodies_sim()/build_quad_worlds_sim() now take a BackendDesc, defaulted to {} so every pre-existing CPU call site is unchanged) with BackendDesc{kind=vulkan, workgroup_size=64 (the compiled default -- see 'workgroup_size' below)}. Per-pass GPU timing is new too: compute/vulkan/timestamps.hpp's PassTimestamps records a Vulkan timestamp query around each of physics/schedule.cpp's 8 schedule slots, baked into StepRecorder's already-once-recorded command buffer (record-once compliance: the query pool is reset and rewritten by the SAME recorded chain on every resubmit, so 'results read per submit' is literally true) and read back through the new Simulation::vulkan_pass_durations_ns() diagnostic accessor -- the same shape as the pre-existing vulkan_step_witness()/vulkan_grid_entries() accessors. Every GPU benchmark below reports six of PassDurationsNs's eight fields (medium_update/force_elements/collision_static/collision_dynamic/integrate/sensor_synthesis, nanoseconds) as custom counters; Gravity and Publish are omitted because they are PROVABLY zero (no dispatch is ever recorded for either slot on either backend), not because they were skipped. ALL NINE FAMILIES BELOW (the pre-existing three plus these six) were re-measured together in ONE spade_bench invocation, foreground, with no other GPU-touching process running on the box (S6 global constraint: only one device-executing run at a time) -- see 'command' below for the exact invocation, including this task's --benchmark_min_time=1s spread-policy discharge.

_meta.spread_policy: S1-S4 carry ticket (first raised by BM_IntegrateOrientation's >3.5x same-box run-to-run spread), DISCHARGED here. --benchmark_min_time=1s applied to the WHOLE spade_bench invocation -- every family in this run, not only the historically sub-microsecond BM_IntegrateOrientation -- rather than a per-family MinTime() call in bench_core.cpp/bench_sim.cpp: 1s is roughly 64x the ~15.6ms default Windows scheduler tick, so each family's auto-selected iteration count accumulates enough total measured time that one preempted or tick-quantized sample cannot dominate the aggregate, and a single global flag is simpler to state, verify and re-apply than nine per-family source edits that would all need the identical value anyway. This run's BM_IntegrateOrientation instance used 17,920,000 iterations (up from 7,466,667 in the 2026-08-10 seed run, itself over its own then-default ~0.5s floor) -- consistent with the floor actually raising the accumulated measurement window as intended. A SECOND, UNANTICIPATED benefit surfaced during this run: BM_StepPlainBodiesGpu/1000 measures cpu_time as exactly 0 (a GPU-bound benchmark spends its wall-clock time blocked in vkWaitForFences, which Windows does not charge to the calling thread's CPU time), which would make a CPU-time-only stopping criterion chase an unreachable floor forever on that basis alone -- google-benchmark still terminated (1 iteration, real_time recorded), but the resulting items_per_second is reported as the JSON value Infinity (a 'divide a positive number by a cpu_time of zero' artifact, not a benchmark defect); see 'note' below.
_meta.not_validatable_on_this_hardware: Engine design spec section 12's dev-GPU rate target ('batched headless >= 64 worlds x 1kHz faster than real time on the dev GPU') names 'the dev GPU' as the validating device. This program's dev-GPU box (S6 global constraint, 'device' above) is an Intel Iris Plus integrated GPU, not a discrete card -- so whatever this run measures is this iGPU's answer, not a proxy for a more capable device a reader might assume 'dev GPU' means. RECORDED, NOT GATED: a miss (or, as this run shows, a bare pass) on this hardware is a fact about THIS box, user-ratified as a posture rather than a build-breaking gate -- see 'world_substeps_per_sec_verdict' below for the number and 'training_spec_tr12' for why the posture now has a second consumer.
_meta.world_substeps_per_sec_verdict: BM_StepQuadWorldsGpu/64 (the literal 64-world x 1kHz target scene, on the literal dev-GPU device, for the first time in this program's history -- the CPU family's identical shape was previously the only measurable proxy). TWO BASES, both computed from this run's own benchmarks[] entries, same duality the CPU family's spec_comparison below already establishes: (1) cpu_time basis (google-benchmark's default items_per_second/world_substeps_per_sec, neither BM_StepQuadWorldsGpu nor any family in this file calls ->UseRealTime()): world_substeps_per_sec = 629,651.06, clearing the 64,000 floor by ~9.84x. (2) real_time basis (the honest wall-clock reading 'faster than real time' actually asks for): real_time = 49,305,726.30 ns for 50 steps => 1014.08 steps/sec => x64 worlds = 64,901.18 world-substeps/sec, clearing the 64,000 floor by ~1.014x -- A BARE PASS, about 1.4% of headroom. THE VERDICT: HELD, on the basis the target's own wording describes, but with none of the CPU family's ~2.8x margin at S3-seed or the ~9.84x this same run's cpu_time basis suggests -- the round trip's fence-wait/submit overhead (StepRecorder::submit()'s per-step blocking wait, once per one of the 50 steps a single benchmark iteration performs) is the gap between the two bases, and on this iGPU that gap consumes essentially the whole margin the cpu_time basis appeared to offer. Recorded as the honest number this run measured; not gated, per the posture above -- a future device (or a future reduction in per-submit fence-wait overhead) is what would widen this margin, not a rule change here.

_meta.spec_comparison: engine design spec section 12 rate-envelope targets (the engine design spec, now docs/design/superseded/kat-originals/kat-spade-engine-design.html, restated in docs/design/superseded/2026-09-consolidation/02-engine.md section 11; quoting closely, not claiming byte-for-byte verbatim -- the source is HTML markup, this is a transliteration of its text): 'single world >= 10 kHz substeps CPU for a quadrotor-class scene ... batched headless >= 64 worlds x 1 kHz faster than real time on the dev GPU. Misses trigger design review, not silent acceptance.' CPU FAMILY (unchanged in kind from the 2026-08-10 seed, re-measured this run): BM_StepQuadWorlds/1's items_per_second (699,935.14 substeps/sec, cpu_time basis) clears the 10 kHz floor by ~70x; BM_StepQuadWorlds/64's world_substeps_per_sec (395,475.86, cpu_time basis) clears the 64,000 floor by ~6.18x. Recomputed on real_time (the basis the batched target's own 'faster than real time' wording actually names): BM_StepQuadWorlds/1 clears 10 kHz by ~69.0x (689,940 substeps/sec from real_time = 72,533.08 ns/iter); BM_StepQuadWorlds/64 clears 64,000 by ~6.09x (389,819 world-substeps/sec from real_time = 8,191,599.11 ns/iter) -- both hold comfortably on either basis, as before. GPU FAMILY (NEW this run -- see 'world_substeps_per_sec_verdict' above for the full account): the batched target is now measurable on its own literal hardware rather than approximated by the CPU twin. BM_StepQuadWorldsGpu/64 HOLDS on real_time (~1.014x, a bare pass) and clears comfortably on cpu_time (~9.84x) -- RECORDED, NOT GATED per the posture above. BM_StepQuadWorldsGpu/1 is NOT compared against the single-world 10 kHz target: that target is stated 'CPU' explicitly in the spec's own words, and a single-world GPU dispatch pays the same per-submit fence-wait/pipeline-bind overhead a 64-world batch amortizes across many more worlds -- BM_StepQuadWorldsGpu/1's low single-world throughput (real_time basis: ~1190.5 substeps/sec) is exactly what a fixed-overhead-dominated single-world GPU dispatch predicts, not a target miss, because there is no GPU single-world target to miss. BM_StepPlainBodies/BM_StepPlainBodiesGpu are not section-12 target scenes either (no vehicle, no IMU) on either backend -- see bench_sim.cpp's header comment for why their points are not directly comparable to each other or across backends (different dynamical regimes, not a regression signal). steps/sec == substeps/sec throughout this file: every Simulation is created with substeps = 1, so items_per_second is reported in substeps/sec directly and needs no conversion.
_meta.note: context/benchmarks below are the UNMODIFIED output of the command above (this file is not hand-edited beyond this _meta block, matching the 2026-08-10 seed's own policy). Two literal artifacts worth naming rather than silently accepting: (1) BM_StepPlainBodiesGpu/1000's items_per_second reads the JSON value Infinity -- google-benchmark computes it as kStepsPerIter*iterations/cpu_time, and this one family's cpu_time measured as exactly 0.0 (see 'spread_policy' above for why a GPU-bound, fence-wait-dominated call does this); real_time (5,062,875,100.04 ns for one 50-step iteration) is the only meaningful throughput basis for this specific data point. (2) The GPU per-pass counters' 'slowest pass' answer depends on the scene: BM_StepPlainBodiesGpu's collision_dynamic dominates OVERWHELMINGLY (e.g. 645,156 ns at N=10 vs medium_update's next-largest 94,115 ns, a ~6.9x gap) -- consistent with that chain issuing several dispatches per substep (grid_build, one dispatch per bitonic sort stage, the sweep) where every other pass issues one, so fixed per-dispatch/per-barrier overhead compounds even though this scene has no actual body-body contacts to resolve (a void world -- see bench_sim.cpp's Sweep 1 header note). BM_StepQuadWorldsGpu's collision_dynamic is still the slowest pass at every world count, but far more narrowly -- at 64 worlds, collision_dynamic (155,521 ns) barely leads sensor_synthesis (149,063 ns, ~4.3% behind) rather than dominating outright, because this scene's collision_dynamic sweep is nearly idle (no contacts; one hover quadrotor per world) while sensor_synthesis pays a real per-substep IMU write for every world's ideal sensor. NEITHER scene in this bench file exercises the 'known posture' the S6 global constraint and this task's brief flag separately -- 'the dynamic-collision Gauss-Seidel sweep is one thread per world ... expect it to dominate contact-heavy shapes' -- because neither builds an actual contact-heavy scene (that is the determinism corpus's 'shower'/'bounce' scenarios' job, exercised for CORRECTNESS by tests/test_gpu_parity.cpp's GpuParityTest.ShowerMatchesTheCpuWithinBands and siblings, not for THROUGHPUT by this file). No kernel changes were made in this task; every number here is measured, not tuned.
